hero.headline: Fort Pierce police chief details arrest timeline for ex-officer who tracked woman 382 times
hero.teaser: Police Chief David Smith laid out how a media inquiry on Aug. 7 led to the arrest of former officer Josepher Crutchfield on four felony counts, including consultation with the State Attorney's Office.
hero.body:
Fort Pierce Police Chief David Smith detailed the timeline that led from a media inquiry to the arrest of former police officer Josepher Crutchfield on four felony counts of unauthorized computer access after investigators say he accessed Flock license plate readers and other law enforcement databases 382 times to track his ex-girlfriend. Crutchfield was arrested Sept. 8 and is being held at the St. Lucie County Jail on $80,000 bail.

 Smith said the investigation began Aug. 7 following an inquiry by the media about possible misuse of the license plate reader system. Later that day, Smith placed Crutchfield on administrative leave and immediately revoked his access to all law enforcement systems. By Aug. 10, Fort Pierce Police Department investigators developed additional information to begin a criminal investigation.

 The investigation was conducted by police department detectives in consultation with the State Attorney's Office of the 19th Judicial Circuit, which includes St. Lucie, Martin, Indian River and Okeechobee counties. Crutchfield submitted his resignation Aug. 18 before the case was resolved.

 Between October 2025 and July 2026, Crutchfield accessed the Flock database 382 times to search for the same vehicle license plate using multiple different reason categories for why the license plate was being searched, according to Smith. The searches did not have any meaningful law enforcement purpose. Most of the searches were made while Crutchfield was off duty. The investigation revealed that the registered owner of the vehicle was Crutchfield's former girlfriend.

 Once the misuse of the Flock camera database was discovered, the review was expanded to other law enforcement databases including FCIC, NCIC, DAVID and TLO, where investigators found Crutchfield made additional searches over the last few years to look up people's names and personal information with no legitimate law enforcement purpose. Smith said during the press conference that the badge does not provide immunity from accountability.

 Smith called the incident a black eye for the department. Fort Pierce police have tightened access to the Flock system so only lieutenants and higher ranking officers can now use it, and each search requires approval from one of two deputy chiefs and a case number. The department also cut its data retention period from 30 days to seven days and added a position within the Office of Professional Standards to conduct monthly audits of law enforcement databases. Crutchfield previously faced an Internal Affairs investigation over allegations of sexually inappropriate behavior toward female Fort Pierce police employees in 2021, which resulted in a two-day suspension without pay.

hero.headline: Fort Pierce police chief details arrest timeline for ex-officer who tracked woman 382 times
hero.teaser: Police Chief David Smith laid out how a media inquiry on Aug. 7 led to the arrest of former officer Josepher Crutchfield on four felony counts, including consultation with the State Attorney's Office.
hero.body:
Fort Pierce Police Chief David Smith detailed the timeline that led from a media inquiry to the arrest of former police officer Josepher Crutchfield on four felony counts of unauthorized computer access after investigators say he accessed Flock license plate readers and other law enforcement databases 382 times to track his ex-girlfriend. Crutchfield was arrested Sept. 8 and is being held at the St. Lucie County Jail on $80,000 bail.

 Smith said the investigation began Aug. 7 following an inquiry by the media about possible misuse of the license plate reader system. Later that day, Smith placed Crutchfield on administrative leave and immediately revoked his access to all law enforcement systems. By Aug. 10, Fort Pierce Police Department investigators developed additional information to begin a criminal investigation.

 The investigation was conducted by police department detectives in consultation with the State Attorney's Office of the 19th Judicial Circuit, which includes St. Lucie, Martin, Indian River and Okeechobee counties. Crutchfield submitted his resignation Aug. 18 before the case was resolved.

 Between October 2025 and July 2026, Crutchfield accessed the Flock database 382 times to search for the same vehicle license plate using multiple different reason categories for why the license plate was being searched, according to Smith. The searches did not have any meaningful law enforcement purpose. Most of the searches were made while Crutchfield was off duty. The investigation revealed that the registered owner of the vehicle was Crutchfield's former girlfriend.

 Once the misuse of the Flock camera database was discovered, the review was expanded to other law enforcement databases including FCIC, NCIC, DAVID and TLO, where investigators found Crutchfield made additional searches over the last few years to look up people's names and personal information with no legitimate law enforcement purpose. Smith said during the press conference that the badge does not provide immunity from accountability.

 Smith called the incident a black eye for the department. Fort Pierce police have tightened access to the Flock system so only lieutenants and higher ranking officers can now use it, and each search requires approval from one of two deputy chiefs and a case number. The department also cut its data retention period from 30 days to seven days and added a position within the Office of Professional Standards to conduct monthly audits of law enforcement databases. Crutchfield previously faced an Internal Affairs investigation over allegations of sexually inappropriate behavior toward female Fort Pierce police employees in 2021, which resulted in a two-day suspension without pay.

cards.teaser: Linn Stewart of Indian River County rises before dawn each morning to feed a colony of stray cats, then spends her days volunteering at For the Love of Paws in Fellsmere. The sanctuary provides free pet food to food banks, veterans, and seniors while caring for animals left behind by elderly owners.
cards.body: Linn Stewart, a 75-year-old Indian River County resident, starts her day at 2:30 a.m. driving through the dark to feed her colony of stray cats. After the predawn feeding, Stewart volunteers 60 hours a week at For the Love of Paws in Fellsmere, a sanctuary for pets left behind by senior citizens who can no longer care for them.
